item.mechanism: Chemical short-range order (SRO) creates percolation pathways of HfTi and TiZr clusters (B2 structure) that facilitate phonon transport, increasing lattice heat conductivity despite the general expectation that precipitates scatter phonons.
item.system: HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy (bcc structure, equiatomic 20% fractions)
item.operating_conditions: Temperature 300 K; Monte Carlo steps up to 4.7e6 to establish SRO; non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulation with thermal gradient (0.8T to 1.2T)
item.supporting_observation: The heat conductivity of the random alloy is lower than that of the segregated binary alloys. We find that, in contrast, due to the increase of the conductivity alongside SRO cluster percolation pathways, SRO increases the lattice heat conductivity by around 12 %.
item.scope_limits: The authors note that this result is expected to be general but explicitly state it was not tested for other alloys in this work; the mechanism relies on the specific formation of HfTi and TiZr clusters which may not occur in all HEAs.
item.alternatives_considered: Phonon scattering by SRO precipitates, which was expected to reduce scattering times and decrease thermal conductivity.
quotes: With increasing SRO, a tendency of forming HfTi and TiZr clusters is found.
Phonon scattering by SRO precipitates might be expected to reduce scattering times and, therefore, decrease thermal conductivity.
due to the increase of the conductivity alongside SRO cluster percolation pathways, SRO increases the lattice heat conductivity by around 12 %.

item.mechanism: SRO modifies the high-frequency part of the phonon density of states (VDOS) by restoring features (peaks and gaps) characteristic of the ordered binary clusters (HfTi, TiZr) that were wiped out by lattice distortion in the random alloy.
item.operating_conditions: 300 K; comparison between random alloy and SRO alloy after 1 million MC steps; analysis of velocity auto-correlation function
item.supporting_observation: Chemical SRO modifies the high-frequency part of the phonon density of states. Due to the strong lattice distortions, the structures within the optical band are destroyed and only a featureless VDOS is left over. With the onset of SRO, the highest peak of the optical band – present both in HfTi and TiZr at around 7 THz – starts to show up.
item.scope_limits: The effect is specific to the high-frequency part of the VDOS (6–8 THz); low-frequency modes (f^2 behavior) are virtually unchanged by SRO.
item.alternatives_considered: The random alloy state where mass disorder and force-constant disorder cause phonon broadening and destroy optical band structures.
quotes: Chemical SRO modifies the high-frequency part of the phonon density of states.
Due to the strong lattice distortions, the structures within the optical band are destroyed and only a featureless VDOS is left over.
With the onset of SRO, the highest peak of the optical band – present both in HfTi and TiZr at around 7 THz – starts to show up.

item.mechanism: The formation of B2 ordered structures reduces lattice distortion (atomic displacements), which reduces phonon scattering and helps increase thermal conductivity.
item.operating_conditions: 300 K; comparison of random vs. SRO samples after relaxation; analysis of pair correlation function and atomic displacement histograms
item.supporting_observation: SRO reduces the lattice distortion thanks to the formation of the B2 ordered structures and, therefore, this would help increasing the thermal conductivity. SRO reduces the width of the g ( r ) peaks.
item.scope_limits: The text notes that while SRO reduces distortion, the random sample still has large displacements (~0.0173 nm) compared to thermal values (0.007 nm), and the mechanism is specific to the reduction of distortion via B2 ordering.
item.alternatives_considered: Large atomic displacements related to anharmonicity and disorder which generally lower thermal conductivity.
quotes: SRO reduces the lattice distortion thanks to the formation of the B2 ordered structures and, therefore, this would help increasing the thermal conductivity.
As expected, SRO reduces the width of the g ( r ) peaks.
This is shown in Fig. S2 a and gives mean displacement values of 0.0173 nm and 0.0153 nm, for random and SRO samples.

item.mechanism: Percolation of HfTi clusters (B2 structure) creates a macroscopic conductive path, where the cluster size distribution follows a power law behavior characteristic of a percolation transition.
item.operating_conditions: Monte Carlo evolution up to 4.7e6 steps; analysis of cluster volume fractions and sizes; 3D site percolation model
item.supporting_observation: All these clusters display a jump in the associated volume fraction at the same time, slightly before 1e5 MC steps, which can be associated with a percolation threshold. There is a clear jump and saturation above 5e4 MC steps, which can be associated with the percolation phase transition.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism relies on the specific HfTi association being the conductive species; other pairs like NbTa are not favored and do not form the percolating path in this potential.
item.alternatives_considered: Random sequential adsorption (out-of-equilibrium process) vs. thermal percolation (equilibrium process dependent on temperature and potential).
quotes: This association will be considered as the conductive (white) species, while any other species as non-conductive (black), reducing the problem to a two-color percolation.
All these clusters display a jump in the associated volume fraction at the same time, slightly before 1e5 MC steps, which can be associated with a percolation threshold.

item.mechanism: High-frequency phonons (wavelength < 1.25 nm) can cross the HfTi B2 substructure without significant scattering once percolation occurs, contributing to the increased conductivity.
item.operating_conditions: Analysis of filament diameters and VDOS; comparison of phonon wavelengths to cluster features
item.supporting_observation: Figure 5 indicates that phonons with wavelength < 1.25 nm will have no problem crossing the HfTi B2 substructure after percolation occurs. This includes most relevant phonons according to the VDOS.
item.scope_limits: This applies specifically to phonons with wavelengths smaller than the filament diameter (~1 nm); the text implies longer wavelengths are less affected or affected differently.
item.alternatives_considered: Nanoscale features generally affecting thermal conductivity due to high-frequency phonon interaction, but here the interaction is non-scattering due to percolation.
quotes: Figure 5 indicates that phonons with wavelength < 1.25 nm will have no problem crossing the HfTi B2 substructure after percolation occurs.
This includes most relevant phonons according to the VDOS (see top axis in Fig. 7 b and c).
SRO features are of the order of 1 nm, in agreement with experimental studies for HEA.

item.mechanism: Chemical short-range order (SRO) leads to the formation of ordered B2 clusters (specifically HfTi and TiZr) which have higher intrinsic thermal conductivity than the random alloy matrix; as these clusters grow and percolate, they create continuous high-conductivity pathways, increasing the overall lattice thermal conductivity.
item.system: Equiatomic bcc HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy with varying degrees of chemical SRO generated via Monte Carlo steps.
item.operating_conditions: Temperature of 300 K; simulated via Molecular Dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC) Kawasaki exchange processes up to 4.7 million steps.
item.supporting_observation: The simulated thermal conductivity increased by 12% (from 0.765 to 0.86 W/(Km)) with maximum SRO, correlating with the volume fraction of ordered B2 phases.
item.scope_limits: The effect is specific to systems where ordered precipitates have higher conductivity than the matrix; it does not apply to alloys where precipitates have lower conductivity (e.g., Si in Al). The authors note this is a 'thermal' percolation driven by exchange processes, not classical random percolation.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered that lattice distortion usually reduces conductivity and that analytical models (Slack, Cahill) based on elastic constants fail to predict this increase. They also considered that phonon scattering at boundaries usually reduces conductivity.
quotes: The increase can be quantitatively explained by a simple composite model, where the material is assumed to be a combination of several phases, each with different heat conductivity.
The phases correspond to the various SRO binary alloys, which have higher thermal conductivity than the random alloy matrix, leading to the net conductivity increase.

item.mechanism: The vibrational density of states (VDOS) changes with SRO, developing structure in the high-frequency part of the spectrum due to optical bands in HfTi and TiZr clusters, which correlates with the increase in thermal conductivity.
item.system: Equiatomic bcc HfNbTaTiZr alloy evolving from random to short-range ordered states.
item.operating_conditions: Simulated at 300 K; VDOS analyzed for samples with varying MC steps (up to 1 million).
item.supporting_observation: The VDOS of the random alloy is a structureless plateau, while the SRO alloy shows structure in the high-frequency part correlated with optical bands in HfTi and TiZr.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism is specific to the phonon contribution; the authors note that electronic contributions were not the focus, though they expect electrical conductivity might also increase with SRO.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors note that long-range ordered crystals show localized peaks, whereas the random alloy has merged acoustic and optic bands without a gap.
quotes: With increasing SRO, the VDOS of HfNbTaTiZr shows structure in the high-frequency part of the spectrum.
A detailed analysis correlates this structure with the optical bands in HfTi and TiZr.

item.mechanism: The formation of ordered SRO phases reduces atomic displacements (lattice distortion) by approximately 12.5%, which contributes to the observed increase in thermal conductivity compared to the highly disordered random state.
item.operating_conditions: Simulated via MD and MC; comparison between random and SRO states (4.7e6 MC steps).
item.supporting_observation: SRO leads to a 12.5% reduction of the atomic displacements due to the formation of ordered phases.
item.scope_limits: The authors state that the increase in conductivity is 'not related to changes in elastic constants', suggesting the reduction in displacement is a distinct factor from elastic property changes.
item.alternatives_considered: Lattice distortion is generally associated with a reduction of thermal conductivity, but here the ordering reduces the distortion, leading to the opposite effect.
quotes: Lattice distortion has been associated to a reduction of the thermal conductivity [33] , [35] .
We observe that SRO leads to a 12.5% reduction of the atomic displacements due to the formation of ordered phases.
This increase is not related to changes in elastic constants.

item.mechanism: Thermal conductivity in this system exhibits a nearly constant value with temperature (decrease < 7% from 300 K to 1300 K) because the SRO and random states lack the strong temperature-dependent phonon scattering mechanisms seen in fcc HEAs.
item.system: Equiatomic bcc HfNbTaTiZr (random and SRO states).
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures of 300 K, 1000 K, and 1300 K; simulated via MD.
item.supporting_observation: The decrease at high temperatures is less than 7% compared to room temperature, unlike the calculations for the fcc HEA which show a 50% decrease.
item.scope_limits: This behavior is specific to the bcc HEA studied; the authors note that fcc HEAs show a strong decrease. The simulation results might only apply to a single-phase bcc HEA as phase changes (hcp) occur in experiments at high temperatures.
item.alternatives_considered: Experiments on sintered HfNbTaTiZr show similar constant conductivity, but other refractory HEAs or fcc alloys typically show significant decreases.
quotes: The decrease at high temperatures is less than 7% compared to room temperature, unlike the calculations for the fcc HEA [32] .
Therefore, there is a nearly constant conductivity, even for the very low level of correlated disorder in the random alloy.
Conductivity does not decrease significantly with temperature for the random or SRO samples, unlike the strong decrease observed for a random fcc HEA [32] .

item.mechanism: The effective thermal conductivity of the SRO alloy can be modeled as a composite of the random matrix and ordered B2 phases (HfNb, HfTi, TiZr, Ta) using a 'mixed model' (harmonic mean of serial and parallel limits) with a weighting factor beta.
item.system: Equiatomic bcc HfNbTaTiZr with SRO phases (HfNb, HfTi, TiZr, Ta clusters) in a random matrix.
item.operating_conditions: Simulated values compared against composite models; volume fractions of phases determined via SurfaceMesh analysis.
item.supporting_observation: The mixed model with beta = 0.65 accurately describes the data, bracketing the simulated heat conductivities as the HEA evolves with MC steps.
item.scope_limits: Simple serial or parallel models alone do not fit the data; the model assumes the material is a combination of distinct phases with different conductivities.
item.alternatives_considered: The Maxwell model for a binary system showed reasonable agreement, but a more realistic model requires many distinct components.
quotes: The increase can be quantitatively explained by a simple composite model, where the material is assumed to be a combination of several phases, each with different heat conductivity.

item.mechanism: Percolation theory explains the sharp increase in thermal conductivity: as the largest HfTi cluster grows and reaches a percolation threshold (around 10^5 MC steps), a spanning cluster forms, drastically changing the transport properties.
item.system: Equiatomic bcc HfNbTaTiZr alloy evolving via MC Kawasaki exchange.
item.operating_conditions: Simulated up to 4.7 million MC steps; percolation threshold identified around 10^5 steps.
item.supporting_observation: The evolution of the largest cluster size indicates a percolation transition, reflected in the number of filaments, atomic coordination, and fractal dimension (Fisher exponent τ = 2.19).
item.scope_limits: This is described as a 'thermal' percolation driven by exchange processes, not strictly 'classical' random percolation, though it belongs to the same universality class.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors note that the percolation transition is not driven by non-equilibrium deposition (RSA-type) but by the exchange process.
quotes: The fact that the growth of HfTi B2 clusters with the number of MC steps is related to an increase in thermal conductivity is explained here by the presence of a percolative transition.

item.mechanism: Analytical models based on elastic constants (Cahill, Slack, mixed-conductivity) fail to predict the SRO-induced increase in thermal conductivity because they do not account for the specific phase separation and cluster formation effects.
item.system: Equiatomic bcc HfNbTaTiZr (random and SRO samples).
item.operating_conditions: Elastic constants evaluated via DFT/MD; thermal conductivity calculated from these constants.
item.supporting_observation: The mixed model and Slack model values are about 7–8 times larger than the MD values; analytical models do not take into account SRO except for possible elasticity changes.
item.scope_limits: These models work for perfect crystals but present limitations for SRO samples where the microstructure is inhomogeneous.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors note that other refractory HEAs give similar lower limits, but the discrepancy with MD results points to pitfalls in using these models for SRO.
quotes: These analytical models do not take into account SRO except for possible elasticity changes, failing to predict an increase in conductivity due to SRO.
The mixed model and the Slack model values are about 7–8 times larger than the MD values.

Recent studies [33] , [34] used the Slack model to estimate the phonon thermal conductivity for many HEAs, but the large discrepancy found here with MD results points to possible pitfalls in this approach.

item.mechanism: The increase in thermal conductivity due to SRO is detrimental to radiation resistance because it prevents the natural decrease of conductivity with temperature, which is needed to cool collision cascades and aid defect recombination.
item.system: Equiatomic bcc HfNbTaTiZr and similar bcc HEAs.
item.operating_conditions: High temperature environments relevant to collision cascades (near melting); radiation resistance context.
item.supporting_observation: The authors argue that SRO causes an increase in conductivity and avoids a decrease at high temperatures, which would be detrimental to radiation resistance compared to alloys that decrease conductivity.
item.scope_limits: The authors note a competing effect where SRO phases might help trap defects, so the net outcome requires detailed study.
item.alternatives_considered: Ab-initio simulations for bcc HEAs show a lowering of electronic thermal conductivity with temperature, which would help radiation resistance.
quotes: Therefore, it would be of interest to design HEAs not only with low conductivity, but also with a decrease in conductivity with temperature.
From this work, SRO causes an increase in the conductivity, together with possible contribution to avoid a decrease at high temperatures.
From the above, this would be detrimental to radiation resistance. However, there is a competing effect, given that SRO phases might help trapping defects and facilitating their recombination.
